title: Budesonide Enteric-Coated Capsules for Children With IgA Nephropathy or IgA Vasculitis Nephritis
off: A Real-World Study of Budesonide Enteric-Coated Capsules in the Treatment of IgA Nephropathy and IgA Vasculitis Nephritis in Children

officials.a: Children's Hospital of Nanjing Medical University
Children's Hospital of Nanjing Medical University

summary: Children with IgA nephropathy, or with IgA vasculitis that has affected the kidneys, often lose protein in their urine, and over many years this can damage the kidneys. Steroid medicines are commonly used to reduce the inflammation, but in children they can cause serious side effects, including slowed growth. This study will give budesonide enteric-coated capsules once a day, for 9 months, to 20 children who also receive standard treatment that does not include steroid tablets. To see whether the capsules help, these children will be compared with 20 similar children who were treated at this hospital in the past and who did not receive the capsules; their information will come from their medical records and their names will not be used. The capsules are approved for adults only, so their use in children is outside the approved label. We will measure protein in the urine and check for side effects.
desc:
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide and is particularly frequent in East Asia; in a Chinese series of 13,519 renal biopsies, IgAN accounted for 45% of all primary glomerulonephritis, and 20% to 40% of affected patients progress to end-stage kidney disease within 20 to 30 years. IgA vasculitis (formerly Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is the most common small-vessel vasculitis in children, with an annual incidence of 3 to 27 per 100,000 children, and 20% to 54% of affected children develop nephritis. IgAN and IgA vasculitis nephritis share mesangial IgA deposition and behave as two expressions of one disease spectrum. Because both usually begin in childhood and last a lifetime, a treatment that controls proteinuria without the toxicity of long-term glucocorticoids is a pressing need in paediatric nephrology.

Current standard treatment combines renin-angiotensin system blockade with glucocorticoids and, in selected children, additional immunosuppressants. In children, prolonged glucocorticoid exposure carries a heavy cost: growth suppression, obesity, hypertension, glucose intolerance, behavioural change and adrenal suppression. Budesonide enteric-coated capsules were designed to avoid this trade-off. The capsule releases the drug in the distal ileum, where Peyer's patches are concentrated, and roughly 90% of the absorbed dose undergoes hepatic first-pass metabolism, so that local mucosal immunomodulation is achieved with limited systemic exposure. In the NefIgArd phase 3 trial, 9 months of treatment reduced proteinuria by about 50% and slowed the decline in eGFR, and the Chinese subgroup showed a 66% reduction in the rate of eGFR loss and a 52% reduction in proteinuria; the 2025 KDIGO guideline and the 2025 Chinese adult guideline both recommend the drug as first-line disease-modifying therapy for patients at risk of progression. Paediatric evidence, by contrast, consists of an 8-patient retrospective case series, a real-world series of six children and a conference abstract; none of these had a concurrent comparator.

This is a single-centre, open-label, real-world study with two components. The treatment group is enrolled prospectively: every eligible child seen at our hospital between 1 December 2026 and 30 September 2027 who gives written informed consent is started on budesonide enteric-coated capsules and followed for 36 weeks. The comparator group is assembled retrospectively from medical records: 20 children with IgAN or IgA vasculitis nephritis treated at the same hospital between 1 January 2020 and 30 November 2026 who did not receive budesonide are matched 1:1 to the prospective participants. Four variables must match: the same sex; the same age in whole years at treatment initiation; the same baseline disease severity, defined by a 24-hour urinary protein stratum (below 1 g/day, 1 to 3.5 g/day, above 3.5 g/day) together with a comparable eGFR stratum (90 or above, 60 to 89, 30 to 59 mL/min/1.73 m2); and the same Oxford MEST-C score on all five items (M0/M1, E0/E1, S0/S1, T0/T1/T2, C0/C1). Matching is performed without replacement by nearest neighbour in the order pathology, severity, age and sex, with a caliper of 0 years for age. Where a full match cannot be found, criteria are relaxed in a fixed order (pathology, then severity, then age to within 1 year, then sex); every relaxation is reported with the number of pairs affected and examined in a sensitivity analysis. No participant is randomised, and no assignment is made by preference: the two groups differ by calendar time, not by chance.

Budesonide enteric-coated capsules are taken once daily before breakfast for 36 weeks at a weight-stratified dose: 4 mg below 16 kg, 8 mg from 16 to below 33 kg, 12 mg from 33 to below 55 kg, and 16 mg at 55 kg or above. If proteinuria disappears completely within the first 3 months, the dose may be tapered to alternate days; if relative remission has not been achieved by month 3, defined per protocol as a fall in proteinuria of at least 50% from baseline together with an absolute value below 0.5 g/day and a stable eGFR, an immunosuppressant may be added. Treatment continues to 36 weeks, or until proteinuria resolves. The dose may be reduced if glucocorticoid-related adverse effects occur. The product is approved for adults only, so its use in children aged 7 to 18 years is outside the approved label.

Eligible children are 7 to 18 years old and able to swallow a capsule, have biopsy-proven IgAN or IgA vasculitis nephritis, meet the protocol criteria for glucocorticoid therapy based on the Oxford MEST-C score and on proteinuria persisting after renin-angiotensin system blockade, have an eGFR of at least 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, and give assent with guardian consent. Twenty participants are planned. No formal power calculation was performed; the sample size reflects feasibility and the size of previously published paediatric series, and the study is exploratory.

Participants attend 10 visits, at baseline and at weeks 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32 and 36, at which blood and urine are collected and height, weight and blood pressure are recorded. The primary outcome is the change from baseline in 24-hour urinary protein excretion at week 36, expressed both in grams per 24 hours and as percentage change. Secondary outcomes are the changes from baseline at week 36 in the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, serum albumin, eGFR calculated with the Schwartz formula (0.413 x 88.4 x height in cm / serum creatinine in micromol/L), urinary red blood cells per high-power field, blood pressure, height and body weight. Adverse events and serious adverse events are recorded throughout.

Analyses will use the full analysis set and the per-protocol set; because no participant is randomised, the intention-to-treat framework is not used. Results will be summarised descriptively, continuous variables as mean and standard deviation, median and interquartile range, minimum and maxi

arms.d: Every eligible child who gives written informed consent is enrolled in this group and receives budesonide enteric-coated capsules once daily before breakfast for 36 weeks, at weight-stratified doses of 4, 8, 12 or 16 mg, together with standard treatment that excludes systemic glucocorticoids, and supportive care with the maximum tolerated dose of an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker. The dose is tapered to alternate-day dosing if proteinuria resolves completely, and an immunosuppressant may be added if relative remission is not achieved by month 3.

arms.l: Historical control: standard treatment, generally including glucocorticoids (retrospective)
arms.d: The comparator group is assembled retrospectively from medical records. Each prospective participant is matched 1:1 to a child with IgA nephropathy or IgA vasculitis nephritis treated at the same hospital between 1 January 2020 and 30 November 2026 who did not receive budesonide. Matching requires the same sex, the same age in whole years, the same baseline 24-hour proteinuria stratum together with a comparable eGFR stratum, and the same Oxford MEST-C score on all five items (M0/M1, E0/E1, S0/S1, T0/T1/T2, C0/C1). Standard treatment for these participants is ascertained retrospectively from the medical record for the 36 weeks after treatment initiation and generally includes oral prednisone 1.5 to 2 mg/kg/day (maximum 60 mg/day), tapered after 4 weeks, together with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker. No budesonide is given.

primary.m: Change from baseline in 24-hour urinary protein excretion at week 36

x.titre: Budésonide gastro-résistant chez l'enfant atteint de néphropathie à IgA ou de néphrite du purpura rhumatoïde
x.question: Le budésonide gastro-résistant réduit-il la protéinurie des enfants atteints de néphropathie à IgA ou de néphrite du purpura rhumatoïde, par rapport à un groupe historique traité par la prise en charge habituelle ?
x.contexte:
La néphropathie à IgA est la glomérulonéphrite primitive la plus fréquente au monde, en particulier en Asie de l'Est. Dans une série chinoise de 13 519 biopsies rénales, elle représentait 45 % des glomérulonéphrites primitives, et 20 à 40 % des patients évoluent vers l'insuffisance rénale terminale en 20 à 30 ans. Le purpura rhumatoïde (vascularite à IgA) est la vascularite des petits vaisseaux la plus fréquente chez l'enfant, et 20 à 54 % des enfants atteints développent une néphrite. Les deux maladies partagent des dépôts mésangiaux d'IgA et sont considérées comme deux expressions d'un même spectre.

Le traitement standard associe le blocage du système rénine-angiotensine et une corticothérapie, parfois complétée par d'autres immunosuppresseurs. Chez l'enfant, la corticothérapie prolongée expose à un retard de croissance, une obésité, une hypertension, une intolérance au glucose, des troubles du comportement et une insuffisance surrénale. Le budésonide gastro-résistant libère le principe actif dans l'iléon distal, riche en plaques de Peyer, et environ 90 % de la dose absorbée subit un premier passage hépatique : l'effet immunomodulateur est surtout local, avec une exposition systémique limitée. Dans l'essai de phase 3 NefIgArd chez l'adulte, 9 mois de traitement ont réduit la protéinurie d'environ 50 % et ralenti le déclin du DFG ; les recommandations KDIGO 2025 le proposent en traitement de fond pour les patients à risque de progression. Chez l'enfant, les données se limitent à de petites séries rétrospectives sans comparateur.

Cette étude monocentrique ouverte comporte un groupe traité inclus de façon prospective (20 enfants, 36 semaines de traitement) et un groupe témoin historique de 20 enfants du même hôpital traités entre 2020 et 2026 sans budésonide, appariés 1:1 sur le sexe, l'âge, la sévérité (protéinurie, DFG) et le score MEST-C d'Oxford. Il n'y a pas de randomisation : les groupes diffèrent par la période, ce qui limite la comparabilité. L'étude est exploratoire, sans calcul de puissance. Le budésonide est utilisé hors AMM chez l'enfant, à une dose adaptée au poids (4 à 16 mg par jour).
x.interet: L'étude pourrait fournir une première comparaison, même non randomisée, du budésonide gastro-résistant à la corticothérapie systémique chez l'enfant. Elle renseignera la faisabilité et la tolérance, notamment sur la croissance, avant un éventuel essai randomisé.
x.profil: Des enfants de 7 à 18 ans atteints de néphropathie à IgA ou de néphrite du purpura rhumatoïde prouvée par biopsie.
inclusion: Âge de 7 à 18 ans, capable d'avaler des gélules
Néphropathie à IgA ou néphrite du purpura rhumatoïde prouvée par biopsie
Indication de corticothérapie selon le score MEST-C et la protéinurie persistante sous blocage du système rénine-angiotensine
DFG estimé ≥ 30 mL/min/1,73 m² (formule de Schwartz)
Consentement signé (assentiment de l'enfant et accord des parents)
exclusion: Infection active nécessitant un traitement antiviral ou antibiotique
Hypertension sévère ou diabète non contrôlés
Autre maladie auto-immune, déficit immunitaire primitif ou cancer
Infection chronique active (EBV, CMV, tuberculose) pouvant être aggravée par les corticoïdes
Insuffisance hépatique sévère, insuffisance cardiaque ou insuffisance rénale terminale

bras.traitement: Budésonide gastro-résistant 4, 8, 12 ou 16 mg/j selon le poids, avant le petit-déjeuner, 36 semaines, avec traitement standard sans corticoïdes systémiques
Prise en charge habituelle, en général prednisone 1,5 à 2 mg/kg/j (max 60 mg/j) avec IEC ou ARA2, sans budésonide

x.critere: Variation de la protéinurie des 24 heures entre l'inclusion et la semaine 36
